transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-15 14:00 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Sara Kim (Redwood AE), Miguel Torres (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood CSM), James Liao (Redwood Support); Aisha Patel (NeuroScale CTO), Ben Ross (NeuroScale SRE), Liam Chen (NeuroScale ML Eng), Grace O'Connell (NeuroScale PM)

Summary: quick follow-up on last week's intermittent timeouts/5xxs. We dug into where requests are queuing, discussed rate-limit behaviour, backoff/retry patterns, and options (temporary traffic shaping, increase reserved concurrency, or move to a dedicated pool). Agreed action items: run controlled burst tests with debug telemetry and share sanitized traces.

Topics: 1) Incident recap and hypothesis, 2) Telemetry gaps, 3) Retry/backoff playbook, 4) Traffic shaping + fallback models, 5) Next steps and scheduling.

--- Transcript body (timestamps approximate; auto-transcript, may contain errors) ---
[00:00] Sara Kim: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. quick roll call, and then we'll go into the incident follow up. Miguel and Ben already exchanged a few logs earlier so thanks for that.
[00:18] Aisha Patel: Yep, hi all. We saw a pretty nasty blip last Thursday where a batch of long-generation jobs started getting 504s then a cascade of 5xxs. That knocked our ingestion pipeline for about 12 minutes.
[00:33] Miguel Torres: Yeah I saw those traces. initial thought: head-of-line blocking in the serving runtime due to a few very long seq requests, combined with the autoscaler not bringing extra capacity fast enough. Also saw signs of KV cache thrash for some request prefixes.
[00:51] Ben Ross: To add, our nginx logs show some queuing at the front end — request queues spiking and client-side retries piling up. We had client retry configured with linear backoff which amplified the surge.
[01:12] Liam Chen: The models in the pilot were running at ~3.2k tokens on average but we had a handful at 18k tokens which I think dominated. we didn't have prefix caching turned on for a couple of those flows because they were multi-turn with dynamic prefixes.
[01:29] Sara Kim: ok good. let's walk through the sequence we think caused the incident. Miguel?
[01:35] Miguel Torres: Sure. Hypothesis: 1) a few long-hold generation requests enter the queue, 2) the runtime does batching and those long requests increase batch latency for other requests (H-O-L), 3) autoscaler sees tail latency, but by the time new workers are up the client retries have already re-flooded the system, 4) backends return 5xx (oom/timeout variants) as memory/KV-caches get evicted. There was also a small region failover we noticed which briefly reduced capacity.
[02:05] Grace O'Connell: Is that region failover related to our VPC peering? we did see a short network flurry.
[02:12] James Liao: The networking event was minor, but it coincided with higher concurrency which exacerbated the downstream effects. Not a full outage, more like capacity wobble.
[02:24] Aisha Patel: Our business impact: the ingestion lagged and some downstream alerting fired. We can't have repeated blips like that during prediction windows.
[02:32] Sara Kim: Totally understood. few levers we can pull immediately and others that are medium-term. we'll separate them into client-side, runtime config, and infra.
[02:44] Miguel Torres: Client-side: implement exponential backoff + jitter (we recommend capped exponential with base 200ms, cap at 10s), add a short idempotency token for dedupe, and prefer fast-fail on 429s to route to a fallback model. Also, implement request-scoped header X-Request-Type to let the runtime do pathing for long vs short requests.
[03:15] Ben Ross: Where would that header be inspected? in the LB or at the Redwood runtime?
[03:21] Miguel Torres: At the runtime layer — it can opt to route 'long' requests to a small dedicated worker pool or to a quantized lower-cost variant. we can also enable early KV-cache lookup to short-circuit some tokens. note: the header is advisory, won't be trusted unless you control client side.
[03:45] Liam Chen: On our side, we can mark long-run requests at the caller and set a higher timeout. But we also need a plan for concurrency limits per request type.
[03:56] Sara Kim: Infra-side: short term we can bump reserved concurrency for your pilot pool, or enable a temporary dedicated pool for long-gen jobs. Medium term: tune autoscaling thresholds and pre-warm workers during peak windows.
[04:15] Aisha Patel: Dedicated pool costs more; how much are we talking for a two-week ramp test?
[04:21] Sara Kim: I'll send estimated numbers after the call. for reference, we have a 'dedicated burst' option that spins up a 4-GPU pool on short notice for X hours/day. price depends on GPU profile.
[04:36] Grace O'Connell: Could we do traffic shaping first? like cap concurrency on certain endpoints and route overflow to a lower-latency model?
[04:42] Miguel Torres: Absolutely. We can add a circuit-breaker at the API gateway that responds with a 429 when excess concurrency is observed and then client can choose fallback. That prevents retry storms.
[05:00] Ben Ross: Our previous setup had a low concurrency limit and the client retry policy was naive — linear 1s increment — that caused hammering. We'll switch to exponential + jitter and also add a request id header so we can dedupe server-side.
[05:21] Liam Chen: Question: does Redwood expose per-request debug sampling or trace ids we can correlate?
[05:27] Miguel Torres: Yes, we can toggle 100% debug sampling for a short window and we inject X-Redwood-ReqId in logs. we'll also output batch composition info for each request in the debug trace.
[05:40] Aisha Patel: that would be really helpful. we need to replay the exact sequence. We'll sanitize and share the example prompts.
[05:48] Sara Kim: Great. on the 5xx types, Redwood noticed both backend timeouts and OOM-like traces in the runtime. Miguel, can you explain what OOM signals we saw?
[05:58] Miguel Torres: Sure. Some of the traces show the runtime evicting KV cache pages and GC pressure rising — not full GPU OOMs but host OOM on CPU process managing KV. That produced internal 5xxs while the worker recycled. Coupled with the long jobs those workers got a skew in memory use.
[06:20] Ben Ross: I remember we had a config that kept KV cache size conservative; maybe it needs bumping for this workload.
[06:28] Miguel Torres: Yes either bump cache size for the pilot or enable per-tenant cache partitioning so long requests don't evict others' prefixes. There's a tradeoff with memory and cost.
[06:40] Liam Chen: Any low-latency mitigations while we test? like a quantized smaller model as a fallback?
[06:47] Miguel Torres: We can route to a 4-bit quantized variant that matches semantics for many prompts; it reduces memory and compute per request — good for fallbacks. It may change some output quality but for interim it's acceptable.
[06:59] Aisha Patel: we are okay with a slight quality delta for non-critical requests. But for paid customers we need strict quality.
[07:05] Sara Kim: noted. so plan: run controlled tests with debug sampling and two variants: 1) current config with increased client-side backoff, 2) traffic-shaping + fallback routing to quantized model. We'll compare tail latency and error rates.
[07:26] Priya Nair: I'll coordinate scheduling. we propose a 2-hour window where Redwood enables 100% tracing and you run bursts.
[07:33] Ben Ross: can we also get a recommended retry-playbook doc? the one you shared earlier was a bit generic.
[07:40] Miguel Torres: yes i'll tailor the retry playbook with numbers we've discussed (base 200ms, cap 10s, jitter, idempotency tokens) and add routing hints. i'll share a PDF and a short YAML snippet you can drop in the client.
[07:54] Aisha Patel: Also, is there a way to separate long-run requests at the LB so they don't hit the same worker queues?
[08:00] James Liao: we can implement route-level pathing: long requests to /v1/long-gen, short to /v1/fast-gen and the runtime maps those endpoints to different worker pools. requires a little client change but doable.
[08:14] Grace O'Connell: That seems attractive — low lift on our side and protects the fast path.
[08:19] Miguel Torres: note: if the client mis-tags a request, it's advisory. we'd still need server-side heuristics that detect long tokens and migrate. there's a tradeoff in complexity.
[08:33] Liam Chen: can we have Redwood produce a short script to re-run these bursts so our ops team can reproduce locally?
[08:39] Miguel Torres: yes. we'll provide a small repro harness plus the benchmark CSV and the commands to run in k6 or locust.
[08:48] Aisha Patel: great. about the autoscaler — you mentioned pre-warming. how long is the spin-up for a new worker?
[08:55] Miguel Torres: depends on GPU type; from 30s to a few minutes. the bulk of time is loading model weights and warming KV caches. we can pre-pull weights if you provide a predictable window, reducing to ~30-60s.
[09:14] Ben Ross: so pre-warm during the 15 minutes before our morning prediction window would likely stop the majority of tail events.
[09:20] Sara Kim: exactly. embedding that into a scheduled scaling policy is straightforward. we'll document it.
[09:28] Grace O'Connell: On compliance: we need to ensure debug traces don't leak PII. how does Redwood handle trace sanitization?
[09:35] James Liao: we scrub request bodies in debug mode by default unless you explicitly enable full payload capture. for this run we recommend sanitized traces. Liam, please sanitize before upload.
[09:48] Liam Chen: will do.
[09:51] Aisha Patel: any quick wins we can do immediately after the call?
[09:55] Sara Kim: switch client retry to exponential with jitter, add X-Request-Type header for long vs short, and Ben enable request-id logging and send sample logs. We'll do a small 15-minute smoke test today if you want.
[10:08] Ben Ross: we can do that after this call.
[10:12] Miguel Torres: i'll prepare the tailored retry-playbook and the traffic-shaping config snippets. also adding a short YAML for the autoscaler pre-warm window.
[10:22] Aisha Patel: Okay, timeline sounds good. one more Q: what's the impact on cost if we spin a short 4-GPU burst pool?
[10:30] Sara Kim: depends on GPU type; rough ballpark is $X/hr per GPU for burst instances. i'll include numbers in the follow-up email.
[10:40] Grace O'Connell: Please include the single-day and two-week estimates so we can justify.
[10:44] Sara Kim: noted.
[10:46] (several minutes of clarifying Q&A about specific log lines and which traces to extract — omitted for brevity)
[30:12] Miguel Torres: quick note — during the earlier incident we saw a small percentage of 502s that correlated with a third-party storage flakiness. we recommend adding a short circuit to avoid repeated reads during that window.
[30:28] Ben Ross: yep that was an S3-like storage hiccup for prefix retrieval. we will add local retries and short-circuit on 5xx from the store.
[30:35] Sara Kim: wrapping up — agreed next steps are in action items. we'll reconvene after the test window and review the patched telemetry.
[30:44] Aisha Patel: thanks everyone. appreciate the quick turnaround.
[30:49] Sara Kim: thanks, we'll follow up by EOD with artifacts and invite for the test slot.
[31:00] (call ends)
